name: Almohad Caliphate

fields.foundation: The Almohad Caliphate began not as a dynastic succession or military coup but as a religious reform movement, founded in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco in 1121 CE. Its founder, Muhammad ibn Tumart, was a Berber theologian of the Masmuda who had studied in al-Andalus and the Islamic East. He returned to the Maghreb preaching strict tawhid, the absolute unity of God, and denouncing the ruling Almoravid dynasty as anthropomorphists who ascribed physical attributes to God and tolerated moral laxity. In Ramadan 1121 his followers proclaimed him the Mahdi, the divinely guided redeemer, and he later established his base at Tinmel in the High Atlas. In its early years the movement fought the Almoravids by raids and skirmishes rather than conventional warfare, and in 1130 an Almohad attack on Marrakesh ended in a heavy defeat at the Battle of al-Buhayra; Ibn Tumart died a few months later. His chief disciple Abd al-Mu'min concealed the founder's death for some two years to keep the movement from breaking up, and then emerged as its leader. Abd al-Mu'min, rather than Ibn Tumart, was the true architect of the Almohad state. Over a reign of more than thirty years he steadily overwhelmed the Almoravids, captured their capital Marrakesh in 1147, assumed the title of caliph, the first Berber ruler to do so, and completed the conquest of the Maghreb from Morocco to Tunisia by 1160. From 1146 Almohad forces also crossed into al-Andalus. The absorption of its remaining independent Muslim principalities, the last being the kingdom of Ibn Mardanish in Murcia and Valencia, was completed under his son Abu Yaqub Yusuf I in 1172.
fields.socioeconomy: The Almohad Caliphate governed one of the most economically diverse empires of the medieval world. It took in the agricultural plains of northern Morocco and Tunisia, the pastoral Saharan fringe, and the urban civilisation of al-Andalus with its dense networks of cities, irrigated agriculture and artisan industries. The North African base produced wheat, barley and livestock across the Tell and the Moroccan plains, while trans-Saharan routes in gold and slaves provided revenues from the empire's southern periphery. The Andalusian economy was the most productive part of the caliphate: the irrigated huertas of Valencia, Seville and Murcia yielded agricultural surpluses; Córdoba, Seville and other cities had skilled industries in textiles, metalwork and ceramics; and the maritime trade of the western Mediterranean connected Almohad ports to Genoese, Pisan and Egyptian commercial networks. Seville was the caliphate's Iberian capital under Abu Yaqub Yusuf I. The Giralda, begun in 1184 as the minaret of Seville's Great Mosque and completed under his son, dates from the caliphate's most prosperous years. The Almohad fiscal system imposed heavy demands on subject populations and provoked periodic resistance. The dynasty's religious rigour confronted Jewish and Christian communities with a choice of conversion or exile, and so disrupted the intellectual and commercial networks that had made Andalusian cities the most cosmopolitan in the western Mediterranean. Keeping forces in North Africa and Iberia at the same time severely strained the empire's finances, a standing burden that contributed materially to its eventual fragmentation.
fields.military: The Almohad military was built on the Masmuda Berber tribes that had gathered around Ibn Tumart's movement, supplemented by Zanata and Arab cavalry, Andalusian contingents and later Christian mercenaries. Abd al-Mu'min made this tribal base into a disciplined force through systematic organisation and the ideological motivation of jihad, and with it an army that could sustain the long campaigns needed to conquer both the Maghreb and al-Andalus. The caliphate's military power was at its greatest under Caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur (r. 1184–1199), who won the empire's most celebrated victory at the Battle of Alarcos on 18 July 1195, where his forces crushed the Castilian army of Alfonso VIII. The victory earned him the honorific al-Mansur, "the Victorious", and in the following campaigns his forces devastated Extremadura, the Tagus valley and La Mancha, raiding to the walls of Toledo in the deepest Muslim penetration of Christian territory for generations. Al-Mansur's death in 1199 and the succession of his son Muhammad al-Nasir gave the Christian kingdoms of Iberia time to consolidate and to form a coalition under papal crusading sanction. The result was the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa on 16 July 1212. The combined armies of Castile, Aragon and Navarre, joined by Portuguese and other crusading contingents, shattered the Almohad force; al-Nasir fled the field and died in Marrakesh the following year. The defeat destroyed the reputation for victory that had been a primary source of Almohad political cohesion, and the caliphate began to break up at a quickening pace. Within sixty years it was gone.
fields.governance: Almohad government was pulled between its founding ideology and the practical demands of administering a large and diverse empire. Ibn Tumart had conceived the movement as a theocratic enterprise in which religious correctness, as defined by himself as the Mahdi, justified political authority. The caliph's legitimacy therefore derived from his role as defender and enforcer of true doctrine rather than from genealogy alone. Abd al-Mu'min gave this an institutional form by establishing a hierarchy of Almohad faithful, drawn from the Masmuda and other early tribal adherents, who formed a ruling class distinct from the general Muslim population, alongside trained cadres of talaba who propagated official doctrine. The caliphal court at Marrakesh kept a developed administration in the Andalusian bureaucratic tradition. The dynasty adorned its cities with monuments such as the Koutoubia Mosque in Marrakesh, whose minaret remains one of the finest examples of Almohad architecture, the unfinished Hassan Tower in Rabat, and the Kasbah of the Udayas. Abu Yaqub Yusuf and Yaqub al-Mansur patronised the philosophers Ibn Tufayl and Averroes (Ibn Rushd), making the court a centre of the highest medieval intellectual culture, although al-Mansur briefly disgraced Averroes in 1195 under pressure from conservative jurists. The weakness of the system was its dependence on ideology: authority flowed from the claim that the caliph governed as the legitimate successor of the Mahdi Ibn Tumart. When Caliph Idris I al-Ma'mun publicly repudiated Ibn Tumart's Mahdi status around 1229, in a bid that also secured Castilian military support, he demolished the theological foundation on which Almohad rule rested and hastened the disintegration that followed.
fields.impact: The Almohad Caliphate mattered most in two fields, war and learning. The caliphate mounted the last great Muslim offensive against Christian Iberia, and the Battle of Alarcos (1195) showed that a unified Muslim power could still threaten the advance of the Christian kingdoms. The subsequent defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) was the decisive turning point. After it Muslim political power in Iberia entered terminal decline, leading to the fall of Córdoba (1236), Seville (1248) and, more than two centuries later, Granada (1492). The Almohad court, particularly under Abu Yaqub Yusuf and al-Mansur, was one of the most important centres of philosophical and scientific activity in the medieval world. Averroes, working under Almohad patronage, produced commentaries on Aristotle that transformed European scholastic philosophy when transmitted through Latin translation, influencing Thomas Aquinas and the wider course of medieval Western thought. The Almohad unification of the Maghreb, the only time it was united under a single Berber dynasty, created an administrative and commercial framework inherited by the Hafsid, Zayyanid and Marinid successor states. The Almohad buildings of the western Islamic world have lasted: the Koutoubia Mosque, the Hassan Tower, the gates and walls of Rabat, and the Giralda of Seville are among the finest surviving monuments of medieval Islamic architecture. The Giralda was converted into a cathedral bell tower after the Christian conquest of Seville and has been part of the city's skyline ever since.
fields.decline: The Almohad Caliphate's decline began with a single catastrophic military defeat and quickened through a sequence of institutional failures that cost the empire its territory, its ideology and its political unity in turn. The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 broke the Almohad army and with it the military prestige that underpinned caliphal authority. A dynasty whose legitimacy rested on divinely guaranteed victory could not absorb a crushing defeat without mortal damage to its ideology. The death without heir of the young caliph Yusuf II (r. 1213–1224) produced rival caliphal claimants, provincial governors who allied with Christian kingdoms in exchange for local autonomy, and a rapid loss of territory. Around 1229 came a double blow: the Hafsid governor of Ifriqiya, Abu Zakariya, broke with Marrakesh, and Caliph al-Ma'mun repudiated Ibn Tumart's Mahdi status. The first removed the eastern third of the African domain, and the second demolished the theological foundation of the entire enterprise. The Zayyanids established themselves at Tlemcen around 1236, carving out the central Maghreb, and the fall of Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248) to Ferdinand III of Castile ended centuries of Muslim rule in the cities most closely associated with Andalusian civilisation. By the 1260s the Almohads held little beyond Marrakesh and its surroundings. In 1269 the last caliph, Idris al-Wathiq (Abu Dabbus), was killed in battle against the Marinids, who seized the capital and ended the dynasty that had once ruled from the Atlantic to Tunisia and from the Sahara to the Tagus.
fields.summary: The Almohad Caliphate was the last great unifier of the western Islamic world. Through the philosophy of Averroes, produced under its patronage, it was also an inadvertent catalyst of the European intellectual revival that would eventually transform the global balance of power.
fields.teaser: A Berber Muslim dynasty that ruled North Africa and Iberia, the Almohads imposed a rigorous religious reform while their court patronised philosophers such as Averroes and Ibn Tufayl.
fields.t0: A Berber religious reform movement from the Atlas Mountains that united the whole Maghreb and Muslim al-Andalus.
fields.t1: Its court patronised Averroes, whose Aristotle commentaries reshaped European scholastic thought.
fields.t2: Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 shattered its prestige; the Marinids took Marrakesh in 1269.
fields.dyk: Seville's Giralda, now the cathedral bell tower, was begun in 1184 as the minaret of the city's Almohad Great Mosque.
